summary: Describes the Connectivity Provisioning Profile and a template to capture IP/MPLS connectivity requirements such as reachability and bandwidth, which can help automate service negotiation and activation.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a form a customer fills out to say what kind of network connection is needed, so the provider can set it up quickly.

questions: what is the connectivity provisioning profile
how does cpp automate service provisioning
what are the reachability models in cpp
how is cpp different from traditional service negotiation
subtitle: A template for specifying IP and MPLS connectivity service requirements.

tldr.problem: Network service negotiation between customers and providers traditionally takes weeks of bilateral discussion without a standard way to describe connectivity requirements, slowing down service delivery.
tldr.mechanism: The Connectivity Provisioning Profile (CPP) provides a standardized template capturing IP/MPLS transfer parameters, reachability scope, quality-of-service guarantees, capacity, availability, and other requirements in a technology-agnostic format.
tldr.outcome: Automating service negotiation and activation using CPP reduces provisioning times and helps service and network management systems make better resource allocation decisions.

today: RFC 7297 remains an Informational RFC describing a generic template. It has influenced thinking in the IETF around service models and is referenced in work on intent-based networking and the OpenDaylight controller project, though standardization of CPP as a protocol has not been pursued.

sections.title: The Need for Standard Service Descriptions
sections.content:
Network service provisioning is complex. A customer (which might be an enterprise, a service provider, or another network operator) must negotiate connectivity requirements with a network provider. Traditionally, these negotiations occur through custom bilateral discussions, each time starting from scratch. The process can take days or weeks, even though the underlying technical requirements are similar across customers and use cases.

The Connectivity Provisioning Profile (CPP) abstracts the common set of requirements that customers express: they need connectivity from certain points to certain destinations, with specified performance guarantees, a defined scope of reachability, and guaranteed availability. The CPP transforms these into a standardized, technology-agnostic format that both sides understand, making negotiation faster and opening the door to automation.

The CPP sits at multiple interfaces: the Customer-Network CPI between a customer and their service provider, the Service-Network CPI between applications and network providers, and the Network-Network CPI between peer networks. By providing a common language across these interfaces, CPP enables consistent service negotiation regardless of the business relationship.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of each company writing down what they need in their own way, they all use the same checklist. The network provider can quickly understand what the customer wants and set up the connection automatically.

sections.title: Core Components of a CPP
sections.content:
A CPP captures several interconnected dimensions of a connectivity service. Customer Nodes identify the endpoints that need connectivity (e.g., routers or gateways at customer sites). The Scope defines reachability: which destinations can be reached from which sources. A global scope means the customer can reach the Internet; a restricted scope means only a specific set of destinations or sources is allowed (useful for VPNs and enterprise networks).

Quality-of-Service (QoS) Guarantees specify performance metrics such as one-way delay, packet loss, and delay variation, either as average values or as maximum bounds. Availability clauses state the percentage of time these guarantees apply and what mechanisms (like backup paths) will ensure the service meets that target. Capacity defines the throughput the service must support.

Additional clauses cover traffic isolation (using VPNs for privacy), flow identification (which packets belong to which service), routing and forwarding (whether traffic should take special paths), activation means (how to enable the service) and invocation means (implicit or explicit trigger mechanisms).
sections.plainLanguage: The form asks: where does traffic go, how fast should it travel, how reliable should it be, how much data can it carry, and should different customers' data be kept separate?

sections.title: From Requirements to Implementation
sections.content:
The key innovation of CPP is separating what is needed (the CPP) from how to implement it (technology-specific policies). A customer might say they need QoS guarantees with low latency; the network provider translates this into specific technical actions such as enabling Multiprotocol Label Switching Traffic Engineering (MPLS-TE) to compute dedicated paths, or activating Differentiated Services (DiffServ) to mark and prioritize traffic.

The CPP can be instantiated into a class of service. Rather than creating a new class for each CPP, best practice maps multiple CPPs to a small number of generic service classes, improving scalability. This approach also enables the CPP to guide network dimensioning: operators can count how many CPPs require a certain service level and ensure sufficient resources are provisioned.

CPP is used for both unicast (point-to-point) and multicast connectivity. The template supports three reachability models: 1:1 pipe (point-to-point), 1:N hose (one site to many), and 1:any (any-to-any outbound). Traffic conformation can be specified using token buckets or other mechanisms, with out-of-profile traffic discarded or assigned a lower-priority service class.
sections.plainLanguage: The CPP is like a doctor's prescription: it says what the patient needs (antibiotics) without specifying which brand. The pharmacist picks the specific medicine that fits the prescription.

sections.title: Benefits and Deployment
sections.content:
CPP brings three main benefits. First, it automates service negotiation and activation, reducing from weeks to hours or minutes the time to provision a service. Second, it provides structured information for network management, allowing management systems to understand what services are running and how much traffic they generate, enabling better traffic engineering and capacity planning. Third, it creates a common interface across different vendor platforms, reducing integration complexity in multi-vendor networks.

CPP is flexible about business models: it works equally well when the same administrative entity manages both service and network infrastructure, or when they are managed separately (e.g., a service provider buys connectivity from a network operator). CPP does not mandate how network services are internally implemented; different vendors can use different technologies (QoS signaling, policy routing, VPN tunnels) as long as they meet the requirements the CPP specifies.

The RFC notes that CPP may be used in frameworks such as Application-Based Network Operations (ABNO) where applications need to request network services dynamically, or for the northbound interface of software-defined networking (SDN) controllers.
sections.plainLanguage: When both sides speak the same language (CPP), ordering a network connection works like ordering a pizza: you tell the provider what you want, they confirm they can do it, and they set it up without endless back-and-forth.
